## Quiz time {#dd-quiz}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Quiz

Who has already used **VHDL**, **Verilog or SystemVerilog**, an **FPGA**, or an
**ASIC design flow**?
:::

::: {.callout-note .fragment appearance="simple" icon=false}
## One more question

Who has **never heard of any of them**?

I need to know whether I should panic.
:::

::: {.fragment}
We will use short **SystemVerilog** examples. The concepts do not depend on that
particular HDL syntax.
:::

## Combinational logic: which line runs first? {#dd-combinational}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```systemverilog
module mul_add4(
  input  logic [3:0] a, b, c,
  output logic [8:0] d
);
  logic [7:0] product;

  assign d =
      {1'b0, product} + {5'b0, c};

  assign product =
      {4'b0, a} * {4'b0, b};
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

The assignment to `d` is written first. Does the **adder** execute before the
**multiplier**?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Answer: neither line runs first.**

- The multiplier and adder are active concurrently.
- The adder settles after `product`, but it is not scheduled after it.
- With no register, there is no stored state or clock cycle.
:::
:::
::::

## Bit widths: where does the carry go? {#dd-widths}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```systemverilog
logic [3:0] a, b;
logic [3:0] wrapped;
logic [4:0] exact;

assign wrapped = a + b;
assign exact =
    {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

For `a = 15` and `b = 1`, what values reach `wrapped` and `exact`?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```text
wrapped = 4'b0000   // 0
exact   = 5'b10000  // 16
```

The extra carry exists only when the operands and result have room for it.
**Width is part of the hardware behavior.**
:::
:::
::::

## Registers: when does `q` change? {#dd-registers}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

If `d` changes between two rising clock edges, when can `q` change?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  q <= d;
```
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/register-timing.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-alt="Timing diagram in which d changes between clock edges and q takes each new value only on the following rising edge" width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
**Answer:** at the next rising edge. A register introduces **state** and a
**cycle boundary**; between edges, `q` keeps its previous value.
:::

## Clock quiz: what does 2 GHz mean? {#dd-clock}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

A processor is clocked at **2 GHz**. How much time separates two rising edges?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
$$
T = \frac{1}{f}
  = \frac{1}{2\,\text{GHz}}
  = 0.5\,\text{ns}
$$

The usable logic delay is slightly smaller once register and clock timing are
included.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="68%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/clocked-datapath.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-alt="A source register feeding combinational multiply and add logic before a destination register, with a common clock" width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
The clock says **when state advances**. It does not serialize the gates between
registers; that combinational logic propagates concurrently.
:::

## Hierarchy: instance or function call? {#dd-hierarchy .smaller}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Is instantiating `mul4` inside `mac4` equivalent to calling a software function?
:::

![](assets/images/digital-design/hierarchy-bottom-up.svg){.fragment fig-alt="A multiplier module reused inside a multiply-accumulate module, which is reused inside a processing element" width="100%"}

::: {.fragment}
**No.** Each instance elaborates hardware. Hierarchy names and reuses structure;
synthesis may later flatten those boundaries into one netlist.
:::

## Generate quiz: how much hardware? {#dd-generate .smaller}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

After elaboration, how many `pe` instances exist?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
```systemverilog
genvar row, col;
generate
  for (row = 0; row < 4; row++)
    for (col = 0; col < 4; col++)
      pe u_pe(/* neighbours */);
endgenerate
```

::: {.fragment}
**16 processing elements.**

The loops generate structure during elaboration. They do not execute at run
time.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/systolic-array-4x4.svg){.fragment fig-alt="Four by four systolic array in which A values flow horizontally and B values flow vertically through sixteen processing elements" width="100%"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
**Voila: matrix-multiplication hardware. Easy.**

*Memory, control, routing, timing, and verification are left as details.*
:::

## FPGA: two ways to be programmable {#dd-fpga-models .smaller}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

When the application changes, what changes inside a CPU and inside an FPGA?
:::

![](assets/images/digital-design/computing-models.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-align="center" fig-alt="A Turing machine leading to a von Neumann computer and a cellular automaton leading to an FPGA fabric" width="82%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
**CPU:** change the instruction stream. **FPGA:** change the circuit itself
[@popoff2026frugality].
:::

## FPGA: why "field-programmable"? {#dd-fpga-history}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
![Xilinx XC2064 package. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/xc2064-package.png){fig-alt="Xilinx XC2064 FPGA in a ceramic dual in-line package" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Was the first commercial FPGA programmed only at the factory?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**No. The field is wherever the user is.**

- 1984: Altera EP300, an early reprogrammable logic device.
- 1985: Xilinx XC2064, the first commercially viable FPGA.
- 64 configurable logic blocks, each with two 3-input LUTs.

The configuration could be changed after manufacturing [@ledoux2024thesis].
:::
:::
::::

## LUT6 quiz: how many bits? {#dd-fpga-lut6 .smaller}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

How many configuration bits are needed to represent **any Boolean function of
six one-bit inputs**?
:::

![](assets/images/digital-design/lut6-rom.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-alt="Six LUT inputs forming an address that selects one of sixty-four stored truth-table bits" width="94%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
**$2^6 = 64$ bits.** The six inputs are an address; the selected stored bit is
the output. A LUT is a tiny addressable ROM containing a truth table.
:::

## LUT quiz: what about seven inputs? {#dd-fpga-lut7}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Can one LUT6 represent every Boolean function of seven inputs?
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="69%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/lut7-compose.svg){.fragment fig-alt="Two six-input lookup tables feeding a multiplexer selected by the seventh input" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="31%"}
::: {.fragment}
**No.** Split the truth table:

- one LUT stores the half for `x[6] = 0`;
- one stores the half for `x[6] = 1`;
- a mux selects the result.

Networks of LUTs implement larger functions.
:::
:::
::::

## FPGA: what the bitstream configures {#dd-fpga-fabric .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
![](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-fabric.svg){fig-alt="Simplified FPGA fabric containing configurable logic blocks, DSPs, block RAMs, IO blocks, and programmable routing" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Is a bitstream executed one instruction at a time?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**No. It configures structure.**

- LUT truth tables and register options
- routing switches
- hard blocks such as DSPs and memories
:::

::: {.fragment}
Once loaded, connections stay fixed and signals propagate through the configured
circuit [@popoff2026frugality; @ledoux2024thesis].
:::
:::
::::

## Same HDL, different target {#dd-targets .smaller}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Which result can still be reconfigured after the chip has been manufactured?
:::

![](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-asic-targets.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="0" fig-alt="SystemVerilog synthesized either into FPGA configuration data or fixed ASIC cell and metal geometry" width="100%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
**The FPGA.** An ASIC has no generic LUT fabric or programmable routing left in
the product. Same SystemVerilog, though. One small mercy.
:::

## ASIC: logic becomes geometry {#dd-asic-cells}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**RTL**

```systemverilog
assign y = a | b;
```

::: {.fragment}
Synthesis maps the operation directly to cells from a technology library.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
![Logic schematic of a SKY130 OR2 standard cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-schematic.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Schematic representation of a two-input OR standard cell" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="36%"}
![Physical layout of the same SKY130 OR2 cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-layout-cropped.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Colored GDSII geometry for a two-input OR standard cell" height="350"}
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
Place and route assigns coordinates and metal wires. Fabrication fixes that
geometry.
:::

## Physical design: equivalent is not identical {#dd-asic-layout}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Placed-and-routed floating-point divider. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/gds-divider.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Physical-design view of a routed floating-point divider with standard cells, clock tree, power grid, and signal wires" height="560"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Question

Must two logically equivalent layouts have the same delay, area, and power?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**No.** Physical cost depends on:

- cell choices and placement;
- wire length and congestion;
- clock and power networks;
- the target manufacturing process.
:::
:::
::::

## Keep the questions explicit {#dd-vocabulary}

| Question | Hardware concept | CIRCT boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Which line runs first? | combinational dataflow | `comb` |
| Where does the carry go? | bit-vector width | `comb` types |
| When does state advance? | register and clock | `seq` |
| Instance or function call? | elaborated hierarchy | `hw` |
| How many generated PEs? | replicated structure | `hw` |
| Bitstream or instructions? | configured target | synthesis |
| What becomes fixed? | cells, wires, geometry | implementation |

::: {.fragment}
CIRCT gives these distinctions explicit IR vocabulary before later tools choose
FPGA resources or ASIC cells.
:::
